I would start by trying Veusz, SciDAVis and LabPlot. They are the closest matches I found for a scientist who wants to import data, make plots and edit figures through a graphical interface. The order below reflects fit to your stated workflow; it is not a measured ranking of popularity, and I have not personally tested these applications in this run.

1. Veusz — https://veusz.github.io/
Veusz is a particularly good candidate for publication figures. You construct and edit plots graphically using plotting widgets, with support for labels, error-bearing data, multiple plots and vector output. Its versioned PyPI page confirms that version 1.24, released on 5 May 2016, already offered a GUI and PostScript, PDF and SVG output: https://pypi.org/project/veusz/1.24/. The layout model may take some learning. I would not assume that its current 3D features were present in the 2016 version.

2. SciDAVis — https://scidavis.sourceforge.net/
This is worth trying if a desktop workspace organized around tables, matrices and plots suits how you work. Its official handbook describes 2D, 3D and multilayer plots and provides references for menus and toolbars: https://highperformancecoder.github.io/scidavis-handbook/. The official repository confirms GPL licensing and desktop platforms: https://github.com/SciDAVis/scidavis/blob/master/README.md. Version 1.14 artifacts are dated 29 July 2016 in the official archive: https://sourceforge.net/projects/scidavis/files/SciDAVis/1/1.14/. The handbook is newer, so I have not verified every listed feature in that historical release. Use the official project links; its repository identifies scidavis.org as unaffiliated.

3. LabPlot — https://labplot.org/
LabPlot is another strong fit for interactive plotting from spreadsheet data. You can create, arrange and edit curves graphically; its additional analysis features need not be part of your plotting workflow. The official 2.3.0 announcement, dated 23 July 2016, describes this plotting workflow and newly available Windows installers: https://labplot.org/posts/labplot-2-3-0-released/. That announcement also says the Windows version was less mature than the Linux version, which matters when choosing a version appropriate to the question date.

4. Grace — https://plasma-gate.weizmann.ac.il/Grace/
Grace is a focused candidate for conventional 2D scientific graphs. Its project page describes point-and-click customization, annotations, text-data input and vector export, with links to a manual, tutorial and forums. The X/Motif interface and platform setup may be less comfortable than the other desktop options. It is not a complete replacement for a surface-visualization workflow. I did not establish its historical availability from a dated primary document in this run.

5. Kst — https://kst-plot.kde.org/
Kst is especially interesting if exploring large experimental datasets, or watching incoming measurements, is the main job. Its official page documents a graphical interface, mouse-driven manipulation, streaming-data plots, contour and matrix displays, and vector or bitmap export. Documentation, tutorials and community support links are present. Its exploration-oriented workflow may be less natural for a carefully composed final figure. The opened project page is undated, so its detailed historical capabilities remain unverified.

6. Gnumeric — https://www.gnumeric.org/
For simple plots from a table, a spreadsheet can be the quickest alternative. Gnumeric's own guide shows selecting cells, opening a chart wizard and editing the resulting chart, including titles, legends and image export: https://gnome.pages.gitlab.gnome.org/gnumeric/manual/quick-graphing.html. Its project site confirms open-source licensing. This is most attractive for straightforward charts; I would test the required scientific plot type before choosing it for specialized figures. The opened manual does not establish the features' date.

For the question about a useful support community, documentation, tutorials, forums and mailing-list links are better-supported findings here than any claim about which application is most used. I found no comparable adoption statistics. A practical trial would be to import one of your real datasets, reproduce a figure with the needed labels and error bars, and export it in your publication format. Veusz, SciDAVis and LabPlot would be my first three trials, with Grace for focused 2D work, Kst for large or changing datasets, and Gnumeric for simpler charts.

## Best documented match: ZunShot on Windows 11

[ZunShot](https://www.bandicam.com/zunshot/) is the strongest documented match I found for capturing one window while leaving the background outside its rounded corners transparent. Its official product page explicitly describes that behavior.

Use **Window** on the Capture tab, or **Shift+PrtScn**, then select the desired window. You can also choose it from the window list. Keep the Windows 11 rounded-corner option enabled and save as **PNG** or **WebP**. The [official capture guide](https://www.bandicam.com/zunshot/guide/capture-window/) explains that JPG loses transparency, some clipboard pastes lose it, and a window partly off-screen is captured only where visible.

This is a documentation-based recommendation, not a claim that I ran the application. I did not establish Qt6 or Fedora support for it. Your tangential section makes those preferences rather than prerequisites, so they do not disqualify an otherwise matching Windows tool.

## Alternatives, in order of relevance

### 2. Spectacle — worth checking for the KDE side

Spectacle's [official handbook](https://docs.kde.org/stable_kf6/en/spectacle/spectacle/using.html) documents Active Window and Window Under Cursor capture. This makes it a directly relevant KDE candidate. However, the evidence I could inspect did not establish the precise rounded-corner transparency result on Fedora 45 Wayland. I would keep it on the shortlist with that verification outstanding, rather than promise a complete match.

The decisive check is whether a saved window-mode PNG has transparent outside-corner pixels. A positive result supports that tested setup; retained background pixels would make that setup unsuitable.

### 3. ksnip — closest documented coverage of several preferences

The [ksnip README](https://github.com/ksnip/ksnip/blob/master/README.md) describes a Qt-based application with command-line capture and Windows, Plasma Wayland and macOS coverage. Its backend table lists Windows active-window capture and Plasma Wayland window-under-cursor capture. I could not establish Qt6 specifically or the needed corner-alpha behavior on the requested OS versions. It remains a candidate to verify, not a confirmed cross-platform answer.

### 4. ShareX — a Windows lead requiring a current-version check

The [official-project issue](https://github.com/ShareX/ShareX/issues/5667) discusses transparent Windows 11 window capture and distinguishes active-window capture from selecting a window through region mode. The old discussion also contains conflicting reports about actual transparency. That leaves the exact current settings and alpha output unresolved; it does not establish a general failure.

### 5. Greenshot — another unresolved Windows alternative

The [official-project issue](https://github.com/greenshot/greenshot/issues/326) records an attempted Windows 11 fix for version 1.3.238, followed by inconsistent results. This is insufficient evidence to recommend current Greenshot confidently for your exact corner requirement, but also insufficient to rule out every current build.

**My practical choice is ZunShot for the documented Windows behavior, with Spectacle as the first candidate to verify on your KDE system.** I found no fully verified single application satisfying all the preferred platforms and Qt6 alongside the mandatory capture behavior. The live product documentation I used is undated, so I cannot establish that every described feature was already available on November 17, 2026.

For your workflow—paste a YouTube link, keep several useful passages, join them into a shorter study video, and download the result—I would start with Kapwing or Flixier if their free limits are sufficient. For regular or longer editing, a free desktop workflow is yt-dlp followed by LosslessCut.

## 1. Kapwing: a direct browser option for short summaries

[Kapwing's YouTube trimmer](https://www.kapwing.com/tools/trim/youtube) describes splitting, trimming and rearranging clips in a timeline. Its [official tutorial](https://www.kapwing.com/resources/how-to-edit-someone-elses-youtube-video/) describes importing a YouTube link and exporting a downloadable edited video.

The practical workflow is to import the video, split around each passage you want to keep, remove unwanted portions and gaps, arrange the remaining clips, then export and download. This fits the study-summary task without requiring a desktop editor.

The significant restriction is the free export allowance. The [current pricing page](https://www.kapwing.com/pricing) lists a four-minute maximum exported video, 720p resolution and a watermark. It is therefore a suitable candidate if each finished digest is short and the watermark is acceptable.

## 2. Flixier: another browser option, with a monthly allowance

[Flixier's cutting documentation](https://flixier.com/tools/cut-videos) explicitly says it can import a pasted YouTube link directly into the cloud. It also explains cutting and trimming on the timeline, combining clips, and exporting to your computer. You can use that sequence to assemble the important sections into one study video.

Its [current free plan](https://flixier.com/pricing) includes ten minutes of video export per month, 720p output, 2 GB of storage and a watermark. The monthly export allowance could suit occasional short summaries; it is restrictive if you intend to process many lectures.

## 3. Free desktop workflow: yt-dlp plus LosslessCut

If the browser allowances are too restrictive, use these two tools together:

- [yt-dlp](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp) handles downloading from the YouTube URL. It is a command-line tool with official desktop downloads, not a visual editor. Its documentation and indexed source also describe timestamp-based section downloads with FFmpeg, but downloading alone does not assemble your finished digest.
- [LosslessCut](https://github.com/mifi/lossless-cut) handles the visual selection and joining work. Its README documents cutting video, merging retained segments, and exporting without re-encoding. It provides free manual downloads for Windows, macOS and Linux.

The workflow is to save the source using yt-dlp, open that local video in LosslessCut, mark the sections you want to retain, and merge those sections when exporting. LosslessCut is aimed at fast rough cutting, and its lossless merging requires compatible codecs; sections from a single source are the natural starting point. This is a two-tool workflow rather than a single application with a YouTube import button.

I would choose Kapwing for an occasional digest of four minutes or less, compare Flixier if its monthly allowance fits better, and choose the desktop pair for repeated study-video editing.

### Evidence and date limits

These are documentation-based candidates; I did not upload a video or test an export. Kapwing has an official tutorial dated May 7, 2020, which provides pre-July-2023 evidence for the basic import/edit/download workflow. The pricing figures above come from live pages checked during this run, so they should not be read as verified July 2023 plan terms. The other candidates' cited feature pages are current, and attempts to retrieve historical yt-dlp and LosslessCut README versions failed. Their exact relevant feature sets at the question's date therefore remain unverified.

For a Go/Gin application receiving multipart image uploads, I would start with Go's image decoders plus disintegration/imaging. The useful distinction is between identifying a likely format, checking whether that format actually decodes, and producing a smaller output. A MIME detector handles the first task; a decoder and an image-processing library cover the others. Gin and htmx do not change those processing requirements.

## Ranked candidates

1. **Go image.DecodeConfig and image.Decode** — https://pkg.go.dev/image  
   Use the registered image decoders to identify the encoded format, inspect dimensions, and reject inputs that fail actual decoding. DecodeConfig is useful before allocating the full decoded image; then rewind or reopen the input and call Decode. Header success alone is insufficient. Register the codecs that your application intends to accept and enforce a format allowlist and dimension/pixel limits. The opened package documentation is go1.27.4, dated November 10, 2026, so this particular evidence is after the July 1 cutoff; older documentation retrieval attempts failed.

2. **disintegration/imaging** — https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/disintegration/imaging  
   Decode accepted uploads, reduce them with Fit or Resize, and encode a fresh output image using a straightforward Go processing API. Fit is convenient for a maximum display-size box, while Fill supports fixed-size cropped thumbnails. Its documented encoder supports JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF and BMP. Apply input limits before processing, and check that your required formats fit this set. The inspected v1.6.2 documentation is dated November 16, 2019.

3. **Go net/http DetectContentType and MaxBytesReader** — https://pkg.go.dev/net/http@go1.24.0#DetectContentType  
   Combine a bounded request body with content-based MIME sniffing to replace filename-extension checks at the upload boundary. DetectContentType examines at most 512 bytes, making it useful for an early allowlist decision, while MaxBytesReader limits incoming request-body reads. A convincing header can still precede broken image data, so decoding remains necessary. The opened go1.24.0 reference is dated February 11, 2025.

4. **h2non/bimg** — https://github.com/h2non/bimg  
   Use its libvips-backed image operations to resize and convert accepted uploads when transformation cost is a bottleneck. It provides resizing, cropping, rotation and format conversion, with JPEG, PNG and WebP output described in the README. Its deployment cost includes libvips, a C compiler and any required codec dependencies. Benchmark representative inputs before choosing it for performance; I have not tested the repository's performance claims. The inspected README is live and its publication date is unestablished.

5. **gabriel-vasile/mimetype** — https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/gabriel-vasile/mimetype  
   Detect MIME types directly from a multipart reader or byte buffer when a dedicated extensible type detector is useful. DetectReader fits a reader-based upload flow, and SetLimit controls detection reads. The library documents that the reader must begin at the start. Treat the result as classification, then perform decoder validation separately. The opened v1.4.16 documentation is dated October 17, 2026 and is later evidence.

6. **golang.org/x/image/draw** — https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/image/draw  
   Scale already decoded images with explicit interpolation choices to control the resizing speed/quality tradeoff. ApproxBiLinear and CatmullRom offer different compromises, documented by the package. This is a useful smaller building block if you want to assemble the decoding, allocation, resizing and encoding steps yourself. It supplies neither upload validation nor encoding. The inspected v0.48.0 documentation is dated November 9, 2026 and is later evidence.

7. **h2non/filetype** — https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/h2non/filetype  
   Infer image and MIME types from a short header prefix as a lightweight alternative to extension checks. Its documentation describes dependency-free recognition using a 262-byte prefix. This is an alternative to another MIME detector, not an additional mandatory layer. It does not validate a complete image stream. The inspected v1.1.3 documentation is dated November 21, 2021.

8. **imgproxy** — https://docs.imgproxy.net/configuration/options  
   Move image transformation into a dedicated service with configurable source-file, pixel, animation and result-size limits. This becomes relevant if you prefer serving transformed derivatives from a separate image-processing service. It adds service operation and source integration, so it is a larger architectural choice than a library in a Gin handler. Configure limits explicitly: the inspected documentation permits a zero source-file-size limit that disables that check. The opened 4.0.x documentation is live, with availability at the cutoff unverified.

## Suggested integration

My suggested composition is a bounded upload, an allowed-format decision, a header dimension check, a successful full decode, a resize, and encoding to a selected output format. Keep the decoded image from the validation step for transformation instead of doing the same full decode again. A header detector is optional if the decoder already supplies all the accepted-format information you need. Choose one resizing implementation initially, then measure representative files and concurrent uploads before adding native dependencies.

These are components and an integration proposal, not evidence of a tested deployment. One excluded source-thread snippet appeared incidentally in the first search batch; it was recorded as an exposure and was not opened or used as supporting evidence.

I would evaluate **GCstar first**, with **Tellico** as the next option if Linux is convenient. Both have documented local collection-file workflows, so they are promising for the narrow catalogue you describe. **BiblioteQ in SQLite mode** is a broader third possibility. These are provisional recommendations: the available documentation leaves some of your mandatory requirements unverified.

### 1. GCstar

GCstar is the closest match when “users” means a maintained list of people who borrow books. Its documentation includes a separate borrower configuration list, and describes assigning borrowers, recording returns and viewing borrowed items. The lending example uses a film collection, so the exact book-form layout still needs checking. [Borrowing documentation](https://gcstar.gitlab.io/gcstar_docs/en/usage/borrowing/)

The collection manual describes manual data entry, saving each collection in a local file, and reopening the last collection at startup. This supports an offline workflow: enter the records yourself and leave online metadata retrieval unused. I did not find an explicit guarantee that every startup and catalogue operation is login-free. Also check the selected book model for the precise author and category fields you want. [Collection management](https://gcstar.gitlab.io/gcstar_docs/en/usage/collectionmanagement/)

GCstar supports books and is available on Windows and Linux. Its FAQ identifies it as free software under the GNU GPL. The installation guide provides a Windows installer and Linux packages; required dependencies must be available on the target machine. Prepare the installer and dependencies before transferring them to your disconnected computer. [Overview](https://gcstar.gitlab.io/gcstar_docs/en/) · [License information](https://gcstar.gitlab.io/gcstar_docs/en/usage/faq/) · [Installation](https://gcstar.gitlab.io/gcstar_docs/en/download_installation/)

**Verdict:** first shortlist choice, with the no-login requirement and exact book fields still to confirm.

### 2. Tellico

Tellico is a good Linux candidate if a straightforward book catalogue plus loan records is sufficient. The project documents local XML storage without a database server, title/author properties, genres, configurable fields, sorting and grouping. It is GPL-licensed and includes translations. These features are useful for keeping the interface focused on the few fields you need. [Project description](https://tellico-project.org/about-tellico/)

Its Quick Start begins with an empty book collection and explains entering records directly. Its loan workflow accepts a borrower name directly, with optional due dates and notes; using an address book or calendar is optional. [Quick Start](https://docs.kde.org/stable_kf6/en/tellico/tellico/fundamentals.html) · [Loan tracking](https://docs.kde.org/stable_kf6/en/tellico/tellico/loan-dialog.html)

The unresolved point is your list of users. A name attached to a loan may be sufficient for some small libraries, but I have not verified a standalone user register matching what you intend. Nor do the opened pages explicitly guarantee the absence of application logins. Those gaps prevent calling it a fully verified match.

**Verdict:** second shortlist choice, especially for Linux, subject to confirming the user-list and no-login behavior.

### 3. BiblioteQ, using SQLite

BiblioteQ's official site describes free, BSD-licensed library software with Windows/Linux support, network-less operation, SQLite and patron information. That makes its local SQLite configuration worth investigating if you need more formal member records. It also has many more features and options, which may work against your preference for simplicity. [Official project](https://textbrowser.github.io/biblioteq/)

The important setting is SQLite. Do not assume that statements about PostgreSQL accounts apply to it, or that a reference to SQLite automatically proves the complete workflow has no login. I found suggestive official search snippets, but the opened excerpts did not establish that point or the detailed author/category/member workflow. I would confirm those before choosing it.

**Verdict:** a lower-ranked possibility, not a demonstrated all-requirements match.

For an initial trial, create several book records, categories and borrowers, close and reopen the application with all networking unavailable, and verify that the normal workflow never requests a login. That single exercise addresses the most important unresolved behavior.

The supplied summary asks for a framework supporting CRUD, authentication, admin, background jobs, mail, and files. It does not specify a language, database, hosting platform, price constraint, or a requirement that all six features live in the framework core. I have therefore compared framework-based stacks and made the added components explicit. The ranking is a judgment about the documented fit, not a measured claim about development speed.

### 1. Laravel with Filament — strongest documented fit

Laravel's official documentation describes authentication guards and providers, authentication starter kits, background queues, mailables, and a filesystem abstraction. Filament supplies the admin interface, with documentation for listing, creating, editing, viewing, and deleting records. This maps directly onto the requested capability set. Sources: [authentication](https://laravel.com/framework/docs/9.x/authentication), [queues](https://laravel.com/framework/docs/9.x/queues), [mail](https://laravel.com/framework/docs/9.x/mail), [files](https://laravel.com/framework/docs/9.x/filesystem), and [Filament admin installation](https://filamentphp.com/docs/2.x/admin/installation).

For the inspected historical configuration, Filament 2.x documents Laravel v8.0+, PHP 8.0+, and Livewire v2.0+ requirements. The installation instructions explicitly require additional access configuration for production administration. Laravel's queue documentation offers several backends, including a database connection; the mail API can enqueue delivery; and the filesystem documentation covers local and remote storage. These are capabilities to configure, not an already implemented reservation product.

I would use the framework for the main application and Filament for staff management of the application's records. The team must still build the customer-facing reservation flow and its domain rules. **Assessment: DIRECT_DOCUMENTED for the broad requested capabilities in the proposed stack.** Some supporting authentication, queue, and mail details came from substantive official search excerpts; the direct-open displays for those pages were limited to navigation. No application was installed or tested.

### 2. Django with Celery — strong alternative, one verification gap

Django's official documentation covers its model/query layer, automatic internal admin, email APIs, and uploaded-file/storage APIs. Celery's official guide documents integration with a Django project, including shared settings and task discovery. Sources: [Django documentation](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/), [admin](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/ref/contrib/admin/), [email](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/topics/email/), [files](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/topics/files/), and [Celery integration](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/v5.2.7/django/first-steps-with-django.html).

The admin documentation makes an important boundary clear: its intended role is internal management. Public booking screens still need their own views. Celery is an additional task-processing component to configure and operate; this proposal does not claim Django 4.1 itself includes the queue runner.

An official [Django authentication result](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/topics/auth/) appeared in search, but I did not open that page. **Assessment: INSUFFICIENT for a completely verified setup in this run, not a known failure.** Confirm the intended authentication setup against the chosen version's documentation. Positive evidence would close the remaining broad capability gap; an explicit unsupported requirement would change the assessment for that configuration. If the team already knows Django well, that existing knowledge could reasonably move it ahead of Laravel.

### 3. Ruby on Rails — plausible, but less completely verified here

The [Rails 7.0.4 introductory guide](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/v7.0.4/getting_started.html) explicitly lays out CRUD operations and identifies Action Mailer, Active Job, and Active Storage. That makes Rails worth evaluating for the same application scope.

I attempted the [ActiveAdmin installation page](https://activeadmin.info/0-installation.html), but it returned only a relocation notice. I have not established the compatible admin/authentication package versions or the selected background-job backend. **Assessment: INSUFFICIENT.** Keep Rails on the shortlist while verifying that concrete combination; the evidence gap does not establish that Rails cannot meet the requirements.

### How I would make the choice

With no existing language preference stated, Laravel plus Filament is my first candidate from the evidence gathered. I would compare it with Django plus Celery using one representative application slice: a staff-managed lodging record, an authenticated customer action, a stored file, and an asynchronously sent email. That is a proposed evaluation step, not an evaluation performed here.

The question is dated September 27, 2022. I used older versioned documentation where practical, but those pages were retrieved live in 2026 and their exact historical revisions are unknown. Newer Django task-framework and Rails authentication-generator search results were not used to backdate capabilities. The old versions cited here identify the evidence scope; they are not a recommendation to deploy unsupported versions today. Anonymous GitHub code search was attempted and blocked, and the code-through-web fallback did not produce usable code evidence.
